teachingPoints.text: The assignment is a bomb-defusal game where one player reads the manual and the other follows those instructions to inspect the bomb and decide which wire to cut.
The bomb exposes discrete parameters - one of three portraits (Lenin, George Washington, Hitler), a wire color, a toggle state and a dial value - and the correct wire is determined from them.
The simplest first step is to store which portrait is currently on the bomb as a string value such as "Ленин" in the program.
A single string variable always holds exactly one of the three portrait names, so its current content tells the player which portrait is displayed.
To verify which portrait is loaded, the program can use that stored string in a check, typing the expected portrait name again.
Statements execute in the order they are written, so running the code as written prints the earlier value first.
Because the portrait variable is overwritten later in the program, a check placed after that assignment never sees the value it expects and therefore does not run.
Placing the check before the later assignment makes it run, because the variable still holds the portrait value the check expects.
String equality in C# compares the two values character by character in order, position by position.
If the expected portrait name is mistyped, the comparison block does not run because the two strings are not fully equal.
Appending extra characters to a mistyped name still fails the check, since string equality requires both the same length and the same characters.
A typo in the expected string is not a compile error, because any string is still a valid string.
A mistyped expected string is also not a runtime error: the program just produces the wrong result and does not crash.
Comparing two strings costs far more operations than comparing two numbers, because the runtime must check the lengths and then walk every character.
The only strong reason to keep the portrait as a string is that the program may need to print which portrait is present as readable text.
The only real need for the string type here is printing the current portrait as readable text.
Storing the portrait as a string risks silently typing the wrong name, and the program gives no visible signal that the string is wrong.
Instead of strings, the portraits can be encoded as integers - Lenin as 0, George Washington as 1 and Hitler as 2 - so the variable becomes a plain int.
With the numeric encoding, whole portraits are represented by single numbers, which removes the possibility of a misspelled name.
Printing the variable now shows the number instead of a name, so a value like 2 does not by itself tell the player it means Hitler.
To keep the human-readable output the program will need a way to convert a number back into text, which is deliberately postponed.
A numeric portrait value must be convertible into its matching text so it can be printed as a string.
The portrait codes are mapped to names by branching on the value: 0 means Lenin and 1 means Washington.
Writing a bare name like Hitler alone is invalid syntax, so the produced text has to occupy the place where the portrait value was passed.
Calling portrait.ToString() returns a string and takes the portrait number as its argument.
The ToString parameter name is independent of the variable name portrait, so any identifier can be used there.
At the print site portrait is replaced by a call that converts it to a string.
An equivalent alternative is to store the converted text in a separate variable and print it in a second step.
The conversion call receives portrait as its argument and evaluates to a string once the argument is computed.
Assigning the conversion result to a variable creates that variable in memory holding the computed string.
Assignment first evaluates the right-hand expression and then puts its result into the variable.
Evaluating the expression makes the code enter the function and pick the matching string, which effectively replaces the call.
Substituting a concrete string for a function call is expression evaluation, which happens when the program runs.
A return statement is needed to declare which string the function expression yields.
Return must be wrapped in curly braces, otherwise the code fails to compile.
Once return executes, the remaining instructions do not run, so trailing else branches can be left out.
If the portrait value is neither 0, 1 nor 2 the function would end without producing a value, so either an error must be raised or a default string such as an empty one returned.
Returning a default empty string is acceptable, but surfacing the error is better so it can be detected during program execution instead of being swallowed.
It is better to let an unexpected value crash the program so the problem is detected immediately during execution rather than disappearing.
Debug.Fail can be used to flag the crash, but the compiler does not recognize it as a crash, so an explicit crash is preferable.
A finished program is expected never to hit this situation, and any such problem should be fixed while developing.
The portrait value is expected a priori to be only one of the allowed values handled by the program.
A well-defined program knows only the three values it handles, so a fourth unexpected value is exactly the case that must be treated as an error.

The lookup function crashes deliberately on any value outside the three portraits it knows, because such a value must never reach it and a debug assertion surfaces the mistake early during development.
If the program knows only about the three values, then any other value must be reported as an error.
Debug.Assert with an explanatory message followed by an empty return runs only in a development build and is stripped out of the final optimized build, so it costs nothing in production.
Running the code shows the value 2 resolving to Hitler, which reveals that the raw integers are magic numbers with no semantic link to the portraits they stand for.
The comment that says 2 means Hitler is only a convention in the source text and has no semantic tie to the program itself.
Introducing constants named for Lenin, George Washington and Hitler replaces the raw numbers so the code states what each value means.
Every place that previously wrote 0, 1 or 2 is rewritten to the corresponding portrait constant, which removes the magic numbers from the logic.
The lesson offers two follow-up improvements: converting the chain of comparisons into a switch, or introducing a separate dedicated type with its own enumeration for the values.
A sequence of ifs that repeatedly compares one value against several constants is exactly the shape a switch expression is meant to replace, as with the earlier if-else chain.
Curly braces should be written after each switch case label so that every case forms its own separate block.
Without those braces a variable declared in one case would be in scope for the whole switch body, so the braces are what prevent that confusion.
A switch whose cases only contain single statements is equivalent to the original chain of ifs, which shows switch is just another spelling of the same branching.
Returning a value from inside switch cases needs a slightly more involved syntax that the lesson defers to a later topic.
Returning from every case is the most common and most useful way to use switch in real programs.
The assignment defines both portraits and a separate set of lamp colors such as Color.Blue, Color.White, Color.Red and Color.Green.
Passing a color where a portrait is expected is meaningless, so the two families of values need distinct types that make such a mix-up impossible.
Each family gets its own specific type, and because an enumeration stores the int values internally, these constants can be defined as enums.
Portrait is declared as an enumeration of int constants, which removes the need to write const int and the type in each field separately.
Enumeration members are separated by commas rather than semicolons and the type name is written only once at the start of the declaration.
Members of the enumeration are now referenced with the type name and a dot, like Portrait.Hitler, exactly as with static class fields, and parameter types become Portrait.
The same enumeration treatment is applied to the lamp colors, which makes both value families equally self-describing.
Applying the same switch-based conversion to colors makes the pattern easier to see than the portrait example alone.
Passing Color.White where a Portrait is expected now fails to compile, confirming that the two types are no longer interchangeable.
With colors wrapped in a dedicated enum type, assigning the bare name Color.White now fails to compile because only values coming from the enum iteration are accepted.
The enum type adds an abstraction layer that hides the numeric backing values, so readers reason about element names instead of magic numbers such as 0, 1, 2.
The function signature is changed to take the Portrait parameter type instead of a plain int, because portrait is no longer an int in the code.
Using the dedicated type in the signature communicates to callers that only the listed portrait values are admissible, which documents the contract in the type itself.
The switch keeps its structure but its default case must stay, because a caller may pass a portrait value that has no explicit case.
Adding a new enum constant creates a value with no matching switch case, so the code can become incomplete just by extending the enum.
Once a constant is added to the enum, user code can pass that new portrait value through the function parameter.
Because the check for the new value is absent, forgetting to add the case crashes the program at run time, and a crash during development points directly at the function and the missing case.
Printing an enum value that has no explicit mapping prints the string constant name rather than the underlying number.
When the enum contains a named constant for the value, the runtime output resolves that value to the constant's name and prints it as a string.
For a value written into the enum, the printed output is the constant name as a string, so a portrait constant prints its name instead of a number.
The auto-printed constant name is an implementation-specific artifact, since it can be Cyrillic or contain spaces, so production code should not depend on it.

Even though an enum can be printed as a constant name, it is often better to define an explicit conversion function, because its text is intended for the user while the implicit name belongs to the program internals.
Because an explicit conversion function returns a Russian label, passing the Lenin portrait prints it in Russian even though the constant itself is spelled with Latin letters.
Even though the portrait is declared as a constant, the compiler substitutes the constant with its numeric backing value 2.
At run time the enum type does not exist and the variable simply stores a plain number, so the enum is purely a compile-time concept in this program.
The enum information exists only at compile time, which is why the compiler can choose to print the constant name rather than the number.
When printing, the compiler picks the constant name from the variable's static type rather than from the stored number, so the same stored value can print differently.
The compiler inserts a numeric comparison for the print operation and performs no string conversion, which is one reason enum values are cheap to work with as numbers.
Enums are used instead of bare numbers because enum members are numbers with meaningful names, so the values stay self-documenting.
The compiler substitutes a constant enum value at compile time, while at runtime the variable's memory cell simply holds that number.
Because the comparison evaluates to true, the guarded block of code executes.
A number that is not one of the enum's declared members can still be turned into that enum type with an explicit cast.
In the example the value 2 is a compile-time constant, so the cast produces the same enum value that was assigned and the equality check succeeds.
The cast can be applied directly to a literal or expression, so converting the number 2 requires no intermediate variable.
An explicit cast performs no validation at all; it simply reinterprets the number as the enum type and stores it in the variable.
A value that is not among the enum's declared constants can still be produced by the cast.
A number absent from the enum's list of constants passes through the cast without any compile-time complaint.
When the program is run, the assignment line executes normally and the program then crashes at the later equality check.
Despite listing only named members, an enum is essentially an ordinary int, which is why a cast can store any integer value in it.
The conversion also works in reverse: casting an enum value to int yields its underlying numeric value.
The example casts the enum to int, prints the resulting number, and then multiplies it by another cast expression.
Predicting the printed result requires working out which subexpression converts to which type and in what order the multiplication is evaluated.
The multiplication can only be evaluated once the value of each of the two operand expressions is known.
The printed result of the multiplication is zero.
The first operand evaluates to zero because the enum member used there has the underlying value zero.
Casting an enum to int returns the numeric value stored for that constant, so the first operand becomes 0.
The second operand's enum constant has the underlying value one, so after casting it contributes 1.
With both operands evaluated, zero times one produces the printed zero.
For an expression of enum type the numeric value is extracted implicitly, which for that constant is 2.
After computing such a numeric expression, the result can be cast back to the enum type if an enum value is needed again.
A broader example of enums in modular arithmetic is deliberately skipped; only the int-conversion trick is required for this video.
The key takeaway is that an enum is just a number, so any manipulation available for plain integers also works on enums.
Enums are plain numbers underneath, so every operation that works on ordinary integers works on them too.
If the first enum member is given the value 0 and later members are left unassigned, each automatically becomes the previous explicitly assigned value plus one.
With members assigned 0, 1 and 2 in order, the implicit rule reproduces exactly that sequence without repeating the numbers.
When only the first member is set to zero, the following members automatically receive 1 and 2 through the previous-plus-one rule.
If the very first enum member is given no value at all, it implicitly becomes zero.
If the first member has no value and the second is explicitly given 5, the second still evaluates to 6 because the implicit value is the previous constant plus one.
The compiler derives each omitted value from the last explicitly assigned constant, which is why the result is 6 rather than 5.
A later enum member can omit its value entirely and still get one more than the previous member, so a count-like member written last takes the number of earlier members.
In the example the count member automatically evaluates to 3, matching the three colors declared above it.
The count constant automatically evaluates to three because three colors were declared above it.
Count is derived from the declared constants rather than typed in, so adding another color constant updates it automatically.
Adding one new color constant is enough to make count become four instead of three.
Count works because each constant is defined from the previous constant's value.

Count does not read the number of array elements; it only takes the last constant's value, which equals the element count because the constants are declared consecutively, each one greater than the previous.
In the code the literal three is replaced by the count constant so the array size no longer depends on a hardcoded number.
Using the constant means adding an enum member such as Yellow only requires one added line, because the consuming code never has to be edited.
The pattern is worth using often because it is common to need an array with one element per enum value.
The count constant is passed to the array constructor to create an array of exactly that size, one entry per color.
